topic: Mood and mental health with PCOS and Hashimoto's: ask to be screened
angle: PCOS guideline says screen every adult for depression and anxiety; Hashimoto's linked with higher odds of both; most Indian women with depression untreated; exercise helps alongside treatment (low-certainty evidence)
hook: If you have PCOS or Hashimoto's, when did a doctor last ask about your mood?
draft:
If you have PCOS or Hashimoto's, when did a doctor last ask about your mood?

It's not just about your hormones. It's about how you feel every single day, and the research backs that up.

The 2023 international PCOS guideline makes a strong recommendation: every adult with PCOS should be screened for depression and anxiety, starting at diagnosis.

For Hashimoto's, a 2018 meta-analysis in JAMA Psychiatry pooled 19 studies and found about three times the odds of depression and about twice the odds of anxiety disorders. These were observational studies, so they show a link, not cause.

In my practice, women usually book for hair fall, weight or tiredness. The full picture comes out later, and many have been managing symptoms quietly on their own.

In India's national mental health survey (2015-16), about 8 in 10 women with depression were not getting treatment. That matters.

Movement is a powerful, evidence-backed tool. A 2024 BMJ review of 218 trials found walking, yoga and strength training all reduced depression symptoms, though the certainty is still low. It works alongside treatment, not instead of it.

What I'd suggest:

- If your mood has changed, tell your doctor, just like any other new symptom.
- If you take medicine for depression or anxiety, talk to your doctor before you change anything.
- If you ever feel unsafe, call Tele-MANAS on 14416, the government's mental health helpline.

How has your mood been lately, honestly?

#PCOS #Hashimotos
final:
If you have PCOS or Hashimoto's, when did a doctor last ask about your mood?

I ask because both conditions are linked with depression and anxiety, and that part rarely comes up in a consultation about reports.

The 2023 international PCOS guideline makes a strong recommendation that every adult with PCOS is screened for depression and anxiety, starting at diagnosis.

For Hashimoto's, a 2018 meta-analysis in JAMA Psychiatry pooled 19 studies. People with the condition had about three times the odds of depression and about twice the odds of anxiety disorders. Those were observational studies, so they show a link and can't tell us which comes first.

In my practice, women usually book for hair fall, weight or tiredness. The full picture comes out later, and many have been managing symptoms quietly on their own for a long time.

In India's national mental health survey (2015-16), about 8 in 10 women with depression were not getting treatment.

Movement can help as well. A 2024 BMJ review of 218 trials found that walking, yoga and strength training all reduced depression symptoms. The certainty of that evidence is still rated low, so I treat exercise as something to add to treatment, never a replacement for it.

What I'd suggest:

- If your mood has changed, tell your doctor, the way you'd mention any other new symptom.
- If you take medicine for depression or anxiety, talk to your doctor before you change anything.
- If you ever feel unsafe, call Tele-MANAS on 14416, the government's mental health helpline.

How has your mood been lately, honestly?

#PCOS #Hashimotos

questions_for_shweta: Line 2 says the mood side 'rarely comes up in a consultation about reports'. Is that true to your experience? If not, I'll cut it to: 'I ask because both conditions are linked with depression and anxiety.'

Alternative hooks: (a) 'The international PCOS guideline says every adult with PCOS should be screened for depression and anxiety. Has anyone screened you?' (b) 'Hashimoto's is linked with about three times the odds of depression. Most thyroid follow-ups only look at the report.'
Comfortable naming the Tele-MANAS helpline (14416)? It's the government's national mental health line.
